label: Implement error propagation strategies across multi agent systems
model: claude-opus-5 (authored in a Claude Code session)

cards.front: What three things does correct error propagation in a multi-agent system require?
cards.back: Structured error context (machine-readable, not a raw exception string), semantic distinctions between failure types (access failure ≠ empty result ≠ transient), and a deliberate partial-result policy (fail entirely vs use what you have).

cards.front: Name the four fields every error crossing an agent boundary should carry.
cards.back: errorType (machine-readable category: access_denied, not_found, timeout, upstream_failure), sourceAgent (which subagent produced it), attemptedAction (the specific operation — tool name, query, step label), and partialResults (data collected before the failure). Plus a human-readable message.

cards.front: Which error field is most commonly omitted, and why does that hurt?
cards.back: partialResults. If a subagent completed 80% of its work before failing, discarding that progress forces the coordinator to restart from scratch. Carrying it forward lets the coordinator choose to resume or discard.

cards.front: Distinguish an access failure from an empty result, and why conflating them is dangerous.
cards.back: Access failure = denied permission, auth boundary, or policy block — retrying with the same credentials won't help, so the coordinator must escalate or skip the source with an explicit annotation. Empty result = the subagent completed successfully and found no matching data — not an error; continue, noting zero records. Conflating them causes either false alarms or a data gap that is invisible to the user.

cards.front: When should a coordinator fail entirely vs use partial results?
cards.back: Fail entirely when the missing subagents hold data that materially changes the answer — the default for correctness-critical aggregations (a financial total from 3 of 5 accounts presented as complete is worse than an error). Use what you have when the failing subagents are supplementary or additive — the default for best-effort enrichment — but you must annotate which sources succeeded, which failed, and why.

cards.front: What is the cardinal rule about partial data?
cards.back: Never silently return partial data as if it were complete. Always set a `partial` flag and include the list of failed sources — a response that LOOKS complete but silently drops failed sources is more dangerous than an explicit error.

cards.front: Why shouldn't a fan-out stop at the first subagent failure?
cards.back: Aborting Promise.all early on a rejection means the coordinator never sees errors from the remaining agents. Run subagents so failures don't short-circuit each other, collect ALL results and errors into an aggregate, then make one decision about remediation.

cards.front: Map each of the four error categories to its decision.
cards.back: Transient (timeout, network, upstream flake) → retry with backoff. Validation (bad input, not_found) → fix and retry, or fail that branch. Permission (access_denied, auth/policy block) → escalate, never retry. Business (valid request the rules reject) → surface or self-correct via isError: true.

cards.front: What are MCP's two error-reporting mechanisms, and how are they handled differently?
cards.back: Protocol errors use standard JSON-RPC errors (error.code, e.g. -32602 unknown tool, malformed request) — clients MAY pass these to the LLM, since recovery is unlikely. Tool execution errors are returned inside a normal, successful tool result with isError: true (input-validation and business-logic errors) — clients SHOULD pass these to the LLM to enable self-correction. Don't confuse the two: isError lives inside the result, not in the JSON-RPC error object.

cards.front: Why is returning a plain string error across an agent boundary an anti-pattern?
cards.back: A string can't carry errorType, sourceAgent, or partialResults, so the coordinator is forced to pattern-match on message text — brittle, and it breaks whenever the message wording changes.
